content: 1. F. Weaver and C. Wilson conducted a study on high-risk indigent families, demonstrating that increasing positive parental behavior support during early childhood can prevent problem behaviors in children. (Child Dev 2008; 79(5): 1395-1414). 2. M. Dozier et al. evaluated a foster parent training program through a randomized clinical trial, finding preliminary evidence that it positively influenced attachment behaviors in young children. (Child Adolesc Social Work J. 26(4): 321-332). 3. D. Drotar, J. Robinson, L. Jeavons, and H. Lester Kirchner assessed the Born to Learn curriculum in a randomized controlled trial, showing its effectiveness as an early intervention program. (Child Care Health Dev 2009; 35(5): 643-649). 4. D.M. Fergusson et al. conducted a randomized trial of the Early Start Program, a home visitation initiative, and found significant benefits for low-income children and their families. (Pediatrics 2005; 116(6): e803-e809). 5. L.C. Fernald et al. demonstrated that group-based parent support within a cash transfer program improved child developmental outcomes in an experimental study. (Developmental Psychology 2017; 53(2): 222). 6. T. Field et al. studied the effects of parent training on teenage mothers and their infants, finding improvements in parenting and infant outcomes. (Pediatrics 69(6): 703-707). 7. E.A. Frongillo et al. evaluated a large-scale behavior-change initiative in Bangladesh, showing advancements in language and motor development among infants and young children. (J Nutr 2017; 147(2): 256-263). 8. J.M. Gardner et al. investigated the combined effects of zinc supplementation and psychosocial stimulation on the development of undernourished Jamaican children, finding significant developmental improvements. (Am J Clin Nutr 2005; 82(2): 399-405). 9. S. Goldfeld et al. assessed the Let’s Read trial, a universal shared reading intervention, and found positive developmental outcomes by age two. (Pediatrics 2011; 127(3): 445-453). 10. B.D. Goodson et al. evaluated a five-year family support program for low-income children, reporting significant developmental benefits. (Early Childhood Research Quarterly 2000; 15(1): 5-39). 11. S. Gowani et al. analyzed the cost-effectiveness of responsive stimulation and nutrition interventions in Pakistan, finding improvements in early child development outcomes. (Ann NY Acad Sci 2014; 1308: 149-161). 12. S.M. Grantham-McGregor et al. conducted the Jamaican Study, which showed that nutritional supplementation and psychosocial stimulation improved the mental development of stunted children. (Lancet 1991; 338(8758): 1-5). 13. D. Gross et al. evaluated the Chicago Parent Program, finding it effective in improving parenting practices among low-income African American and Latino parents. (Prevention Science 2009; 10(1): 54-65). 14. A. Guedeney et al. studied the impact of a randomized home-visiting trial on infant social withdrawal, finding significant reductions in withdrawal behaviors. (Infant Mental Health Journal 2013; 34(6): 594-601). 15. C.L. Guttentag et al. assessed the My Baby & Me program, an early parenting intervention, and found positive effects on at-risk mothers and their children. (Dev Psychol 2014; 50(5): 1482-1496). 16. J.D. Hamadani et al. demonstrated that psychosocial stimulation improved the development of undernourished children in rural Bangladesh. (J Nutr 2006; 136(10): 2645-2652). 17. S.M. Hartinger et al. evaluated a child stimulation intervention in rural Peru, finding significant developmental benefits in a cluster-randomized trial. (J Epidemiol Community Health 2017; 71(3): 217-224). 18. C.M. Heinicke et al. studied a relationship-based intervention for at-risk mothers, showing positive outcomes in the first year of life. (Infant Mental Health Journal 1999; 20(4): 349-374). 19. H. Helmizar et al. found that local food supplementation combined with psychosocial stimulation improved linear growth and cognitive development in Indonesian infants. (Asia Pacific J Clin Nutr 2017; 26(1): 97). 20. C.E. Heubner demonstrated that community-based interventions can promote toddlers' language development effectively. (Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 21(5): 513-535). 21. H. Hiscock et al. evaluated a universal parenting program to prevent early childhood behavioral problems, finding significant benefits in a cluster-randomized trial. (BMJ 2008; 336(7639): 318-321). 22. J. Hutchings et al. assessed the Incredible Years Toddler Parenting Programme in disadvantaged areas of Wales, reporting positive outcomes for parents and toddlers. (Child Care Health Dev 2016; 43(1): 104-113). 23. F. Jacobs et al. evaluated a home-visiting program for adolescent parents, finding improvements in parenting and child outcomes. (Am J Public Health 2016; 106(2): 342-349). 24. X. Jin et al. studied the Care for Development intervention in rural China, showing long-term benefits for child development. (J Dev Behav Pediatr 28(3): 213-218). 25. D.L. Johnson et al. evaluated the Houston Parent-Child Development Center, finding it effective in improving outcomes for Mexican-American families. (Am J Orthopsychiat 44(1): 121-128). 26. F. Juffer et al. demonstrated that early interventions in adoptive families improved maternal sensitivity, infant-mother attachment, and infant competence. (J Child Psychol Psychiatry 38(8): 1039-1050). 27. P.I. Kaaresen et al. conducted a randomized trial of an early intervention program for low birth weight children, finding positive outcomes at two years. (Early Hum Dev 2008; 84(3): 201-209). 28. L. Kalinauskiene et al. evaluated a video-feedback intervention to promote maternal sensitivity and infant attachment security, finding significant benefits. (Child Care Health Dev 2009; 35(5): 613-623). 29. J.W. Kaminski et al. assessed the Legacy for Children public health approach, finding improved behavioral and socioemotional outcomes in children born into poverty. (Am J Public Health 2013; 103(6): 1058-1066). 30. H. Kitzman et al. evaluated the effects of prenatal and infancy home visitation by nurses, finding improvements in pregnancy outcomes, childhood injuries, and reduced repeated childbearing. (JAMA 1997; 278(8): 644-652). 31. G. Kochanska et al. demonstrated that a play-based intervention improved toddlers' social-emotional outcomes in low-income families. (J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2013; 42(5): 700-712). 32. N.M. Kyno et al. evaluated an early intervention program for preterm infants, finding developmental benefits at 36 months. (Infant Behav Dev 2012; 35(4): 916-926). 33. C. Leung et al. assessed the Fun to Learn for the Young Program, finding it effective in improving child outcomes in a randomized trial. (J Child Fam Stud 2017; 26: 2865-2878). 34. J.M. Love et al. evaluated Early Head Start, finding significant benefits for three-year-old children and their parents. (Dev Psychol 2005; 41(6): 885-901). 35. B. Lozoff et al. demonstrated that home interventions improved cognitive and socio-emotional scores in iron-deficient anemic infants. (Pediatrics 2010; 126(4): e884-e894). 36. J. Madden et al. evaluated the Mother-Child Home Program, finding positive effects on mother-child interactions and child development. (Child Dev 1984; 55(2): 636-647). 37. M. McGillion et al. tested the effects of promoting caregiver contingent talk on infant language development, finding significant benefits. (J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2017; 58(10): 1122-1131). 38. A.L. Mendelsohn et al. used videotaped interactions during pediatric well-child care, finding improvements in parenting and child development at 33 months. (J Dev Behav Pediatr 2007; 28: 206-212). 39. P. Menon et al. combined intensive counseling with a mass media campaign, finding differential impacts on complementary feeding practices but not on child growth. (J Nutr 2016; 146(10): 2075-2084). 40. J. Mora et al. demonstrated that nutritional supplementation improved physical growth in children at risk of malnutrition. (Am J Clin Nutr 1981; 34(9): 1885-1892). 41. G.K.M. Muhoozi et al. evaluated a cluster-randomized trial in Uganda, finding that nutrition, hygiene, and stimulation education improved growth, cognitive, language, and motor development. (Matern Child Nutr 2017). 42. L. Murray et al. assessed a book-sharing intervention in South Africa, finding improvements in caregiver-infant interactions and infant cognitive and socioemotional outcomes. (J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2016; 57(12): 1370-1379). 43. B. Nahar et al. demonstrated that a community-based approach combining food and psychosocial stimulation improved growth and development in severely malnourished children in Bangladesh. (Eur J Clin Nutr 2012a; 66(6): 701-709). 44. B. Nahar et al. found that psychosocial stimulation improved home environments and child-rearing practices in a community-based trial in Bangladesh. (BMC Public Health 2012b; 12: 622). 45. M.K.C. Nair et al. evaluated the Child Development Centre Model, finding that early stimulation improved outcomes for at-risk babies. (Indian Pediatrics 2009; 46: S20-S26). 46. K.F. Norr et al. assessed a nurse-health advocate home-visiting program, finding positive maternal and infant outcomes at one year. (Public Health Nurs 2003; 20(3): 190-203). 47. D.L. Olds et al. demonstrated that nurse home visitation programs effectively prevent child abuse and neglect. (Pediatrics 1986; 78(1): 65-78). 48. D.L. Olds et al. compared home visiting by paraprofessionals and nurses, finding significant benefits in a randomized controlled trial. (Pediatrics 2002; 110(3): 486-496). 49. M. Pontoppidan et al. piloted the Incredible Years Parents and Babies Program, finding promising results in a randomized controlled trial. (PLoS One 2016; 11(12): e0167592). 50. C. Powell et al. integrated early stimulation into primary care for undernourished Jamaican children, finding it feasible and effective. (BMJ 2004; 329(7457): 89). 51. V.A. Rauh et al. evaluated an early intervention program for low birth weight children, finding significant developmental benefits over four years. (Child Dev 1988; 59(3): 544-553). 52. M. Robling et al. assessed the Building Blocks program, a nurse-led home-visiting initiative for first-time teenage mothers, finding positive outcomes. (Lancet 2016; 387(10014): 146-155). 53. P.C. Rockers et al. evaluated a community-based intervention package in Zambia, finding significant developmental benefits in a cluster-randomized trial. (BMJ Global Health 2016; 1(3): e000104). 54. L.A. Roggman et al. demonstrated that parenting-focused Early Head Start programs improved attachment security and cognitive development. (Early Education and Development 2009; 20(6): 920-941). 55. M.P. Santelices et al. evaluated an early intervention program in Santiago, Chile, finding improvements in secure attachment among mother-infant dyads. (Child Care Health Dev 2011; 37(2): 203-210). 56. M.G. Sawyer et al. tested an internet-based support program for new mothers, finding it non-inferior to traditional methods in a randomized controlled trial. (J Med Internet Res 2017; 19(7): e258). 57. S. Scarr and K. McCartney evaluated the Mother-Child Home Program in Bermuda, finding significant developmental benefits. (Child Dev 1988; 59(3): 531-543). 58. D.F. Schwarz et al. promoted early intervention referrals through a home-visiting program, finding significant improvements in a randomized controlled trial. (Journal of Early Intervention 2012; 34(1): 20-39). 59. D.S. Shaw et al. found that improvements in maternal depression mediated the effects of an intervention on early childhood problem behavior. (Dev Psychopathol 2009; 21(2): 417-439). 60. D.R. Singla et al. evaluated a parenting intervention in rural Uganda, finding improvements in maternal psychological well-being and child development. (Lancet Global Health 2015; 3(8): e458-e469). 61. S.J. Spieker et al. assessed a relationship-based intervention for toddlers in child welfare, finding significant benefits in a randomized trial. (Child Maltreatment 2012; 17(4): 271-286). 62. F. Tofail et al. demonstrated that psychosocial stimulation benefited development in non-anemic children but not in anemic, iron-deficient children. (J Nutr 2013; 143(6): 885-893). 63. Z. Vally et al. evaluated dialogic book-sharing training in South Africa, finding improvements in infant language and attention. (J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2015; 56(8): 865-873). 64. J. Van Zeijl et al. demonstrated that an attachment-based intervention enhanced sensitive discipline in mothers of young children at risk for externalizing behavior problems. (J Consult Clin Psychol 2006; 74(6): 994). 65. S. Vazir et al. found that complementary and responsive feeding education improved dietary intake, growth, and development in rural Indian toddlers. (Matern Child Nutr 2013; 9(1): 99-117). 66. M.K. Velderman et al. demonstrated that attachment-based interventions improved maternal sensitivity and infant attachment, particularly in highly reactive infants. (J Fam Psychol 2006; 20(2): 266-274). 67. D.P. Waber et al. evaluated the effects of nutritional supplementation and maternal education on cognitive development in infants at risk of malnutrition. (Am J Clin Nutr).
